summary: Presents a checklist for evaluating MIME-capable user agents. It replaces RFC 1820 with an updated version. It is informational.

plainLanguage.summary: A list of things an email program should handle, so you can check off which ones it does.

questions: how to evaluate a mime email client

how to test an email client for mime support
what is the mime test responder
subtitle: A questionnaire for judging how well an email program handles MIME, plus a robot that mails you test messages.

tldr.problem: Buyers, administrators and vendors had no common way to compare how well different email programs (user agents) handled MIME multimedia mail.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC gives a four-part checklist of questions about a user agent and describes an automated responder that mails back sample messages of each content type for testing.
tldr.outcome: It is a practical aid, not a standard: the RFC says it is not a conformance or interoperability checklist, and it replaces RFC 1820.

today: RFC 1844 is an Informational memo that obsoletes RFC 1820 and has not itself been obsoleted or updated. It does not specify a standard of any kind.

sections.title: What the Checklist Is For
sections.content:
RFC 1844 presents a checklist that helps evaluate email user agents (the programs people read and write mail with) that support MIME. It is aimed at users and system managers.

The author is careful about what it is not. It is not a conformance or interoperability checklist, both of which are strictly defined and measurable. It is an interworking checklist, which means it takes a practical perspective on how a product behaves. The document obsoletes RFC 1820.
sections.plainLanguage: It is a list of questions for checking an email program, made for ordinary people who run or buy mail software rather than for lab testers.

sections.title: Submitting Results
sections.content:
Anyone who runs the checklist against a product, whether vendor, implementor or user, can mail the filled-in form to mime-check@nic.surfnet.nl. The subject must reflect the product name and version. The address is an automated mail handler, so only filled-in checklists in content type text/plain or text/html should be sent.

The results were to be published at no cost on a SURFnet web page. SURFnet tried to verify each submission but gave no guarantees about errors or damages. Buyers are told to treat the data as orientation and run their own procurement tests, and vendors are encouraged to use the results to improve their products.
sections.plainLanguage: You fill in the form, mail it to a robot, and your answers go on a public shelf. Nobody promises the answers are perfect, so shoppers should still try the program themselves.

sections.title: Getting Test Messages
sections.content:
Many checklist items need a sample message to test against. You request one by mailing mime-test@relay.surfnet.nl with a subject containing exactly one name from a list. The reply goes to the address in your From field.

The list covers content types such as text/plain, text/enriched, image/gif, image/jpeg, audio/basic, video/mpeg, application/postscript, message/rfc822, message/partial, message/external and the multipart types multipart/mixed, multipart/parallel, multipart/digest and multipart/alternative. It also has three special subjects: X-local (an undefined content type, to see how your agent copes), nested (a message with nested multipart contents) and iso-8859-1 (a text/plain message with that charset).
sections.plainLanguage: There is a robot that mails you one sample of each kind of message, such as a picture or a sound. You open each one to see whether your email program copes.

sections.title: The Checklist Itself
sections.content:
The checklist has four parts. Part 1 collects general facts: product name and version, the manufacturer, supported platforms, whether it comes as source or binary, and pricing (public domain, shareware, non-profit use only, or commercial). Part 2 covers installation, configuration and management, including whether outgoing messages get correct RFC 822 headers (From, Sender, Date, Message-id), size limits, mailbox security and subjective speed.

Part 3 asks about general agent properties: graphical or character interface, the delivery protocols supported (SMTP, ESMTP, POP, IMAP), submission protocols, basic functions such as reply and forward, folders, filters, sorting, address directories and secure mail (PEM, PGP).

Part 4 is the MIME part. It asks whether the agent can view, save and print MIME content, which of the basic content types it can receive and compose, how it handles unknown types, and which encodings it supports: 7bit, quoted printable, base64, binary and 8bit. It also checks that the agent generates Mime-Version: 1.0, what multipart boundary strings look like, whether non-ASCII characters work in headers, and which character sets (such as iso-8859-1) are supported.
sections.plainLanguage: The list asks who made the program, how easy it is to set up, what mail jobs it does, and then which kinds of pictures, sounds and files it can show and send.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content: Testing an agent against this checklist carries the security risks described in the MIME specification, RFC 1521. The RFC singles out one: automatic execution of general-purpose PostScript interpreters entails serious security risks. Readers are pointed to RFC 1521 for details.
sections.plainLanguage: Some message files can contain little programs. If your email program runs them on its own without asking, that can be dangerous, so be careful when testing.
